sources.name: Letter from Sen. Ron Wyden and Rep. Richard Neal

caption:
Two top Democrats in Congress opened an investigation into how the Trump administration let Nvidia sell H200 AI chips to China.
Their letter says the deal gave the government a 25% cut through what they call an unconstitutional export tax.
It also asks why sales continued after warnings about Jensen Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese spy.

Should the US sell its best AI chips to China at all?

site_article.seo_title: Democrats probe Trump's Nvidia H200 chip deal with China

site_article.answer_summary: Sen. Ron Wyden and Rep. Richard Neal opened an inquiry into how the Commerce Department approved Nvidia H200 chip sales to China in exchange for a 25 percent cut, and asked Commerce to preserve all related records.

paragraphs.text: Two senior Democrats in Congress opened an inquiry on November 12, 2026, into the Trump administration's decision to let Nvidia sell its H200 artificial intelligence chips to China. Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, the ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee, and Rep. Richard Neal of Massachusetts, the ranking member of the House Ways and Means Committee, sent a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick describing the arrangement as a scheme to approve and tax the exports.

The letter arrived on the same day Nvidia's board removed Jensen Huang as chief executive. Huang had admitted an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a company U.S. officials suspect of helping route advanced Nvidia chips into China, according to TechCrunch and The Hill.

According to the letter, President Trump allowed Nvidia in December 2025 to sell H200 chips to Chinese buyers in exchange for a share of the sales. The chips, manufactured in Taiwan, were to be shipped to the United States for a security review and an export license before being re-exported to China. The administration used Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 to place a 25 percent tariff on the chips when they entered the country.

Wyden and Neal argue that this tariff functions as an unconstitutional export tax. They write that Congress created Section 232 as a tool for acting against imports that threaten national security, and that its use in this case appears to have had the opposite effect. The Hill notes that the administration had earlier allowed sales of Nvidia's H20 chips to China for a 15 percent cut, a revenue-sharing deal that Nvidia and AMD agreed to in August 2025, according to TechCrunch.

The letter cites reporting by The New York Times that Commerce approved Chinese companies with links to the Chinese government, the military or sanctioned firms, including so-called cutout companies with no physical presence at their listed addresses. It also cites reports that Commerce suspended an investigation into whether Megaspeed smuggled Nvidia chips into China after Nvidia reached out to the department. The Hill reports that the Times said the case may have been passed to the Justice Department, which declined to comment.

The lawmakers also point to reports that Huang and Nvidia directed at least $26 million toward the president's priorities, including the White House ballroom. TechCrunch reports that the letter asks whether those donations were connected to the chip approvals, and why Megaspeed was allowed to keep buying chips after U.S. intelligence reportedly warned Lutnick about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang.

The letter does not include a deadline or a numbered list of questions. It asks Lutnick to preserve all records related to the Section 232 semiconductor investigation, including a December 22, 2025 report to the president, the department's handling of Nvidia's export license applications, and its communications with or about Nvidia and Huang. It reminds the department that destroying records relevant to a congressional investigation is a federal crime.

Because Democrats are in the minority in both chambers, Wyden and Neal can ask questions but cannot compel answers, TechCrunch reports. A separate Republican-led effort involving the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the House Intelligence Committee had demanded that Huang testify in a closed session. After his resignation, Huang agreed to testify. Neither TechCrunch nor The Hill reported a response from Nvidia, the Commerce Department or the White House.

The inquiry moves the Nvidia story from a corporate scandal to a question about government process. The central issue raised by the letter is whether export decisions on the most advanced AI chips were made on national security grounds, or shaped by revenue and political considerations.
The next signal to watch is whether the Commerce Department responds to the preservation request, and what Huang says when he testifies before the Republican-led House committees.
